hits.name: Insomnia
hits.text: A CLUB JUST ASKED MY FLY TO DJ THEIR ENTIRE NIGHT Yesterday I got a message from a club called Neon Hive with a completely insane proposal: they wanted my FLY to run their next party from start to finish and choose everything by itself. They wanted no human controlling the set. So I gave them my code, connected the system to their DJ setup and let the fly take over the booth for the night. From that moment, every decision was hers. Fly picked what played next, controlled the decks and kept the party moving while hundreds of people danced, sang and had absolutely no idea who was actually running the music. The weirdest part is watching the footage afterward. You see a packed nightclub going completely crazy while this tiny fly is sitting behind the decks with its headphones on, casually running the entire night like this is what it was born to do. Nobody in the crowd knows their DJ is an insect. And somehow, the party just keeps going. Neon Hive might have been the first club brave enough to hire a FLY

hits.text: this is straight f*cking gold the full harness guide for Kimi K3, the #1 open source frontend model the premise: the model underneath keeps changing. the harness is the part that stays yours what one night of it looks like: 02:00 - the trigger fires, every node that needs work gets picked > 212 agents fan out, one per node > a bad return gets rejected, retried once with the reason attached > one agent tries to write outside its folder. blocked. nobody woken up > +41 nodes and +96 edges land in the graph > a drafted email hits pre_send and waits for you 02:41 - the loop stops on its own, inside a 45 minute budget 07:30 - you read one file and make two decisions the whole machine is one folder, one config file, five short scripts two rules hold it together: > the model sits behind one line, so a better model is a config change > the verifier lives outside the agent, so nothing grades its own work now the money part companies burn whole quarters building internal agent platforms a harness setup for a small team goes for four figures, one time then a monthly retainer to run the swap test on every new model release models come and go. the person who owns the harness keeps getting paid https://t.co/MA0WCoJp4B

hits.name: cvxv666
hits.media_note: video, 56 seconds; quoted article/video from Aug 6
hits.text: I used GPT-6 Astra to build a neural copy of 169 winning memecoin traders, then handed it money. +$2,088 in a week. ×2.2 on capital. Nobody touched it. 82% of its calls went above entry. It posts every one of them to X and Telegram by itself. Anyone can get the same calls. 139,454 fills. 6,289 tokens. 536 wallets scored. The top one is up $10.8M in 30 days. Still $0 a month in API bills. Every 20 seconds: > READS every fill on Robinhood Chain, 20 seconds behind the block > CHECKS the receipt on each one. 1 in 11 "smart money buys" on this chain is fake, it zeroes them > SCORES every trader 0 to 100 the way the 169 would, reasoning written out > FIRES when trusted wallets pile into one coin inside 30 minutes. 66 calls last week, 54 above entry > TRADES its own bursts. $100 a ticket, 17 tickets, +$2,088 in 5 days > POSTS every call to Telegram 20 seconds after the fill and to X an hour later CATGPT ran ×27 after the call. musebook did ×18 on a $100 ticket and covered all 9 losers of the week. Jane Street has a desk of humans reading trades like this and the results never leave the building. This one puts them on a public timeline an hour later. The site, the bot, the X account and the code are all in my profile. Next the algo goes live on a public wallet, and the flywheel gets its second turn.

hits.name: Insomnia
hits.media_note: video (21 seconds; quoted Google Mapped a Fly article card)
hits.text: I TURNED A FLY INTO A WELDER AND GAVE IT ITS OWN FABRICATION LAB I don't know why this seemed like a reasonable experiment, but now there is a robotic fly standing inside a fabrication workshop operating a live welding arc. The machine moves around the metal surface while a bright arc cuts across it, drawing a pattern one movement at a time. The fly is right there in the middle of the process, moving its mechanical legs and wings while its camera eyes watch the work from inches away. And the setup is way more serious than it has any right to be. The system is running around 85 amps and 12.2 volts, with the thermal array pushing past 1,400 degrees while the wire extension keeps advancing across the surface. Then you look at the other half of the screen. 166,700 retained neurons. 25.5 million approximate synapses. 15,378 neurons fired. The entire connectome is being visualized beside the fabrication process, with neural activity lighting up the brain while the robotic fly is working. So technically this isn't just a fly holding a welding tool. It's a tiny nervous system connected to a machine that can actually build things. I think I just gave a fly its first job in heavy industry

hits.name: NO1ennn
hits.media_note: image (quoted ONE AGENT CREW article card)
hits.text: this is f*cking gold Uber engineers built their own AI coding assistant for six months, then killed it on purpose. 100 million lines across six monorepos. zero new headcount approved. so they pointed agents at the debt instead. every workflow gets modelled as a state machine. deterministic steps call a tool: prepare the mocks, run the build, index the repo. only the steps that need judgement call a model. red CI feeds the error back to the model the same way it would to a person, and it loops until green. the Java to Kotlin migration is where it bites. 10 million lines. on the current trend it finishes in 8 years. so they mined their own history: replay thousands of past migrations, run today's tooling over the same commits, diff it against what the developer actually shipped. that delta is everything the tooling was missing. then the constraint that makes the whole thing safe. the model is never allowed to write the migrated code. it writes the AST rule. the rule is deterministic, gets reviewed once, and converts the repo forever. 8 years becomes 18 months. same cycle on tests. generate, build, fix its own failures, validate the asserts against the comment on the function, refactor into the house pattern. 29 manual steps, one loop, runs to 80% coverage. the leverage was never the model. it was the veto.

hits.name: RetroChainer
hits.media_note: video (16 seconds; quoted Mr. Buzzoni article card)
hits.text: I GAVE KIMI K3 THREE HUNDRED AGENTS AND ONE NIGHT. ZERO WAKE-UPS. four tools. five hooks. budget forty five minutes, finished in forty one. the hooks did the work I used to do by hand: 1,689 tool calls checked before they touched anything 1,689 answers checked on return 21 failures retried with the reason attached 1 draft held in a queue for me 1 run written into the record morning: one file to read, two decisions. seven disciplines everyone named separately are parts of one machine. the prompt is a file. the context is an assembler. the tools are typed. the loop is a runner that stops on counts. the memory is a graph. the check is a verifier the agent does not control. the frame around all of it is the harness. K3 leads the frontend arena right now. 1,679 against 1,631 and 1,618. first in six of seven domains. seventeen places up in one update. which is why it sits behind one line and nothing else in the system knows its name. the swap test: change that line, run the night again. passed. format held, the run still ended on counts, last week's corrections still loaded, nothing wrote outside its folder. whatever breaks after a swap was never the model. it was your harness hiding inside a prompt. save this.

outsiders.video_tip: Cut the long interview into three concrete agent-engineering lessons with bold on-screen chapter cards.
outsiders.hook: Stop polishing prompts; start engineering the agent.

outsiders.name: Ziwen
outsiders.text: Union Alpha is now in Codex!! The speed is insane over 300 to 400 tokens a second, 262k context, images in, and it's free for a week. It's a good timing too, most of the Codex usage is basically gone right now. Zai did this exact thing in August: Ox Alpha showed up unnamed, free for a week, built for agentic coding, and a week later it was GLM-5.3-Flash. So what model do you guys think it is?
outsiders.video_tip: Show the token-speed counter, context window, and image input in a single fast Codex benchmark clip.
outsiders.hook: A stealth model just appeared in Codex at 300–400 tokens per second.

outsiders.name: hammertime
outsiders.text: Wall Street spent decades building $24K terminals and $650K quant teams just for Sam Altman to put a chat box in front of the whole thing.
outsiders.video_tip: Contrast a Bloomberg terminal and quant floor with a single chat box in a punchy visual before/after.
outsiders.hook: The $650K quant team meets the chat box.

outsiders.name: Francesco
outsiders.text: the biggest shift in how ChatGPT actually gets used is happening right now - and almost nobody is talking about it same ChatGPT prompt. same model. monday: 71% successful runs wednesday: 99% not one word changed. we changed the graph around the model. here's the uncomfortable
outsiders.video_tip: Animate identical prompts hitting two different graph layouts with the success rate jumping from 71% to 99%.
outsiders.hook: Same prompt, same model, radically different result.

outsiders.name: 0xMarioNawfal
outsiders.text: This guy built a full website using Claude Opus 5 in a single HTML file with no images, fonts or libraries, every room, person and ink dot drawn entirely in code. Website link: a-small-light-three.vercel.app
outsiders.video_tip: Start with the finished one-file world, then flash the source file and the no-library constraint.
outsiders.hook: An entire interactive world in one HTML file.
